title: Whatever happens next
description: Say what may happen, and what must be done.
grammarNote: The perfect subjunctive is the -se form of the past subjunctive: haya hablado, haya comido.

explanation.summary: The perfect subjunctive is the present perfect with the -se ending instead of the -o ending. It appears in a handful of fixed phrases, and it is the natural way to say that something must happen before something else can.

sections.heading: How it is formed
sections.body: Take the present perfect and change the ending: he hablado becomes haya hablado, has comido becomes haya comido. The forms only exist for haber, which is why you only learn one set: haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayáis, hayan.

examples.en: It is possible that he has arrived.

examples.es: Necesito que hayan enviado el paquete.
examples.en: I need them to have sent the parcel.

sections.heading: Where it appears
sections.body: The commonest use is with esperar, to hope: espero que haya llegado. Then it comes after expressions of doubt and possibility: es posible que, no creo que, es dudoso que. And it says something must be done first: necesito que hayan pagado.

examples.es: Espero que hayáis visto el mensaje.
examples.en: I hope you have seen the message.

examples.es: No creo que hayan llegado todavía.
examples.en: I do not think they have arrived yet.

examples.es: Es dudoso que haya sido posible.
examples.en: It is doubtful that it was possible.

items.note: It introduces a wish: ojalá sea, if only it were.
